sections.content: You know *si bien* + indicative and *aun cuando* and *por más que* + subjunctive from B2 Unit 8: three formal ways to concede. At C1 the concession is a move in the argument. You name the other side's best point, grant it fully, and then show why you still disagree. The objection goes in the concessive clause, and your position goes in the main clause, which is the one that counts. The mood tells the reader how you treat the objection. *Si bien* grants a fact, with the indicative. *Aun cuando* and *por más que* take the subjunctive when the objection is open: something that may happen and will not change your mind.

sections.title: Three ways to grant a point
rows: Si bien la inquietud de los residentes es legítima, la medida no puede esperar.
Although the residents' concern is legitimate, the measure cannot wait. (a fact you grant)
Aun cuando algunos locales vendan menos, el cambio es necesario.
Even if some shops sell less, the change is necessary. (an open point)
Por más que algunos insistan, el centro no puede ser un aparcamiento.
However much some insist, the centre cannot be a car park. (the insisting may go on; it changes nothing)

items.spanish: Ciertamente, la objeción es fundada, pero no cambia nuestra postura.
items.english: Admittedly, the objection is well founded, but it does not change our position.

items.spanish: Si bien el miedo a perder clientes es comprensible, no puede decidir el futuro del centro.
items.english: Although the fear of losing customers is understandable, it cannot decide the future of the centre.

items.spanish: Aun cuando los comerciantes pierdan algunos clientes, la medida sigue siendo necesaria.
items.english: Even if the shopkeepers lose some customers, the measure remains necessary.

items.spanish: Por más que pidan más tiempo, la decisión no cambiará.
items.english: However much they ask for more time, the decision will not change.

sections.content: English "although" does every job. In Spanish write *si bien* with no *que* and no accent (*sí* means "yes"), and *aun cuando* with no accent on *aun*. When you give the other side the point, say so (*Ciertamente…*, *Hay que darles la razón en eso…*), and then do not take it back: the main clause must say what you still believe.
